questions.question: Earth spins around and around on an imaginary line that runs through its centre, from the North Pole to the South Pole. What is this line called?
questions.context: Earth's axis is the imaginary line it spins around, and its two ends are the North and South Poles. The equator is a different imaginary line, running around Earth's middle halfway between the poles, and an orbit is the path Earth travels around the Sun.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 teaches 5th graders that Earth rotates about an axis between its North and South Poles, and that word is the core of every day-and-night lesson.

questions.question: Earth spins steadily, turning around and around without ever stopping. About how long does Earth take to spin all the way around once?
questions.context: Earth spins around once in about 24 hours, and that spin is what a day is. Twelve hours is only about half a turn, 30 days is roughly a month, and 365 days is a year, the time Earth takes to travel all the way around the Sun.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade day-and-night units (curriculum map G5.E1, NGSS 5-ESS1-2) teach that Earth spins once about every 24 hours.

questions.question: A town has hours of daylight, then hours of darkness, then daylight again, over and over without end. What causes this cycle of day and night?
questions.context: As Earth spins, the town is carried into the Sun's light, which is its day, and then around to the side facing away from the Sun, which is its night. Earth does circle the Sun, but one trip takes a whole year, and the Sun does not travel around Earth at all.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 names day and night as a pattern caused by Earth's rotation; Baxter (1989) found pupils from age 9 blaming the Moon, the Sun's travels or Earth's orbit instead.

questions.question: A girl eats her lunch at noon under a bright Sun. At that same moment, what time of day is it for a boy on the exact opposite side of Earth?
questions.context: Only the half of Earth facing the Sun has day. The boy's side faces away from the Sun, so he is in the middle of his night, and his noon will come about 12 hours later.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade day-and-night lessons (NGSS 5-ESS1-2) teach that the half of Earth facing the Sun has day while the other half has night.

questions.question: From sunrise to sunset on a clear day, the Sun seems to travel across the sky. In which direction does the Sun seem to travel?
questions.context: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. It only seems to move: Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun appears to slide the other way across the sky, the way trees seem to slide backward past the window of a moving car.
questions.grade_note: The curriculum map's G5.E1 and NGSS 5-ESS1-2 teach the Sun's apparent path, rising in the east and setting in the west because Earth turns.

questions.question: On a sunny day, a girl's shadow stretches out across the grass in front of her. Which way is she facing?
choices: With the Sun on her left
With the Sun on her right
questions.context: A shadow forms where an object blocks the light, so it always falls on the side away from the Sun. With her shadow in front of her, the Sun must be behind her.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade shadow-tracking lessons (NGSS 5-ESS1-2) start from the rule that a shadow falls on the side of an object away from the Sun.

questions.question: Early on a sunny morning, a stick in a schoolyard casts a shadow that points west. Which way does the stick's shadow point late in the afternoon?
questions.context: A shadow points away from the Sun. In the morning the Sun is in the eastern sky, so shadows point roughly west; by late afternoon the Sun appears in the western sky, so the stick's shadow has swung round to point roughly east.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 asks 5th graders to find the pattern in shadows' daily change of direction, roughly west in the morning and east in the afternoon.

questions.question: A boy measures the shadow of a flagpole every hour on a sunny day, from just after sunrise until just before sunset. How does the shadow's length change?
questions.answer: Long, then short, then long again
choices: Long, then short, then long again
Short, then long, then short again
The same length all day long
Long at first, then shorter all day
questions.context: Shadows are longest early in the morning and late in the afternoon, when the Sun is low, and shortest around midday, when the Sun is highest. Far from the equator the noon shadow never vanishes completely, because the Sun is never straight overhead there.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 asks 5th graders to graph shadows' daily change in length: long in the morning, shortest near midday, long again by evening.

questions.question: On a sunny day, a tree's shadow stretches across a field, many times longer than the tree is tall. Where in the sky is the Sun?
questions.context: The lower the Sun sits in the sky, the more its light comes in at a slant and the longer the shadows it makes, which is why shadows are longest near sunrise and sunset. A high Sun makes short shadows, and a Sun straight overhead would leave almost none.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade shadow lessons tie a shadow's length to the Sun's height in the sky: a low Sun makes a long shadow and a high Sun a short one.
